newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia's Bakun dam poor investment risk - NGOs.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia's Bakun dam poor investment risk - NGOs.

text.p: Malaysia's $5.4 billion Bakun dam is a poor investment risk which has already made potential foreign investors nervous, a coalition of non-government organisations said on Tuesday.

The hydroelectric dam, with a designed capacity of 2,400 megawatts, is being built in the forested interior of Malaysia's Borneo state of Sarawak. Scheduled for completion by 2003, the dam will clear 69,000 hectares of forest and create a reservoir the size of Singapore.
Power will be delivered to peninsular Malaysia via a 670-km cable under the South China Sea, more than double the length of the world's longest existing underwater cable.
Transmission losses on the undersea and overland cables "could well be over 10 percent", the Concerned NGOs on Bakun said in a statement.
Security guards prevented the group from delivering the statement to the Securities Commission chairman.
The statement cited a World Bank study estimating the average capacity factor for hydro-electric stations at 49 percent against Bakun's rated capacity of 74 percent.
"The amount of power that can actually be generated is thus a major risk factor for investors," the statement said.
Bakun Hydro-Electric Corporation (BHEC), the dam's operating company, will list on the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange in June.
The issue, consisting of 1.5 billion shares at two ringgit apiece, would be the single largest flotation on the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange to date.

Ting Pek Khiing, executive chairman of Ekran Bhd, the main contractor of the project, confirmed last week that the 10 percent of BHEC reserved for foreign investors would be open to local institutional investors as well.
Another 15 percent had already been allocated exclusively for Malaysian investors.

Analysts say foreign investor interest in the project has been lukewarm because of its six-year payback period, probable cost overruns, and the higher risks generally associated with dam construction.

The statement pointed to Malaysia Mining Corp Bhd pulling out of the project in November, and Tenaga Nasional reducing its stake to five percent from 25 percent, as signs that local institutions were also wavering.
Bakun would be the largest and highest rock-filled dam in the world.

The state-run Sarawak Electricity Supply Corporation; Tenaga Nasional Bhd, which has agreed to buy most of the power; and the government's investment arm, Khazanah Nasional Bhd, signed a shareholders agreement last week giving them a total of 75 percent of the holdings of BHEC.
The remaining shares will be sold to the public.
The anti-Bakun activists said BHEC is offering only an 11 percent return to investors against an average of 14 percent from the broader stock market.
"There is a major risk that investors will find their returns below expectations and that the shares may fall below their listing offer price," the statement said.
